content: Dicloxacillin is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections caused by specific bacteria. It works by inhibiting the synthesis of bacterial cell walls, which ultimately kills the bacteria. However, it is not effective against viral infections such as the common cold, influenza, or COVID-19, nor is it effective against non-bacterial infections. Resistance to dicloxacillin can occur due to alterations in penicillin-binding proteins, which may reduce its efficacy. Drug Interactions: 1. Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors (e.g., camrelizumab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab, durvalumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, etc.): Dicloxacillin may reduce the therapeutic effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors through an unspecified mechanism. Close monitoring is recommended, as coadministration may interfere with the efficacy of these agents. 2. Cholera Vaccine (live): Dicloxacillin can antagonize the effects of the cholera vaccine. Avoid coadministration with systemic antibiotics, as they may inactivate the vaccine strain. Do not administer the vaccine to patients who have received antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. 3. Oral Contraceptives (e.g., dienogest/estradiol valerate, ethinyl estradiol, levonorgestrel): Dicloxacillin may decrease the effectiveness of oral contraceptives by altering intestinal flora or affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Women should use alternative or backup contraception during concurrent use. 4. Methotrexate: Dicloxacillin can increase methotrexate levels by reducing renal clearance, potentially leading to hematologic and gastrointestinal toxicity. Monitor serum methotrexate levels closely. 5. Tetracyclines (e.g., doxycycline, minocycline, tetracycline): Tetracyclines may interfere with the bactericidal action of dicloxacillin due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid concurrent use or consider alternative therapies. 6. Typhoid Vaccine (live): Dicloxacillin can antagonize the effects of the live typhoid vaccine. Administration of the vaccine should be delayed until antibiotic therapy is completed. 7. Probenecid: Probenecid increases dicloxacillin levels by decreasing renal clearance. Use caution and monitor closely. 8. Chloramphenicol: Chloramphenicol may reduce the effects of dicloxacillin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown, but monitoring is advised. 9. Mycophenolate: Dicloxacillin may decrease the active metabolite of mycophenolate by impairing enterohepatic circulation. Monitor for reduced efficacy of mycophenolate. 10. CYP3A4 Substrates (e.g., pacritinib, tazemetostat, tinidazole, ubrogepant): Dicloxacillin may reduce the levels or effects of these drugs by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Dose adjustments or alternative therapies may be necessary. 11. Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) and Salicylates (e.g., piroxicam, salsalate): Dicloxacillin may interact with these agents by competing for plasma protein binding or reducing renal clearance. Monitor for increased drug levels and potential toxicity. 12. Microbiota Oral Therapy: Dicloxacillin may reduce the efficacy of microbiota oral therapy by antagonizing bacterial spores. Complete antibiotic regimens 2–4 days before initiating microbiota therapy. Side Effects: Common Side Effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and black hairy tongue. Report any bothersome side effects to your healthcare provider. Serious Side Effects: Severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, may occur. Discontinue dicloxacillin immediately and seek emergency medical attention if symptoms such as difficulty breathing, swelling, or rash develop. Other Adverse Effects: Abdominal pain, fever, hypersensitivity reactions, nephritis, pseudomembranous colitis, seizures (with high doses or renal failure), rash (ranging from maculopapular to exfoliative), and superinfections with prolonged use. Pharmacokinetics: Absorption: 35–76%, reduced by food. Protein Binding: 96%. Metabolism: Hepatic (CYP3A4). Excretion: Primarily via urine (56%) and feces. Half-Life: 5–2 hours. Distribution: Widespread, with the highest concentrations in the kidneys and liver; low levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Special Considerations: Pregnancy: Category B. Generally considered safe, with no evidence of fetal risk in controlled studies. Lactation: Excreted in breast milk; use caution. Neonates: Drug elimination is slower; use with caution. Prolonged Use: May result in superinfections. Warfarin Interaction: Monitor prothrombin time (PT) closely if used concurrently. Storage: Store dicloxacillin at room temperature (68–77°F or 20–25°C). It can tolerate short-term exposure to temperatures between 59–86°F (15–30°C) during transport. Dosage Forms: 250 mg oral capsules. 500 mg oral capsules. Dicloxacillin is a penicillinase-resistant antibiotic primarily used to treat infections caused by penicillinase-producing staphylococci. Resistance may develop due to alterations in penicillin-binding proteins.
